title: Mindful Drinking Apps: The Best Apps to Cut Back (Not Quit)
excerpt: An honest comparison of mindful drinking apps for cutting back, not quitting: Try Dry, Drinkaware, Drink Less, DrinkControl, Sunnyside, and Reframe, plus what the research says.
metaDescription: Honest comparison of mindful drinking apps for cutting back: Sunnyside, Reframe, Try Dry, Drinkaware, Drink Less. Free vs paid, pros, cons, and what works.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the best mindful drinking app is the one you'll actually open on a Thursday night. For most people who want to cut back rather than quit, that means a simple drink tracker with a weekly goal. Free options like **Try Dry** (from the UK charity behind Dry January), **Drinkaware**, and **Drink Less** (built by researchers at University College London) cover that well. Paid apps like **Sunnyside** and **Reframe** add coaching, lessons, and nudges, which some people find worth the subscription and others drop after a month. No app will change your drinking on its own. What apps do well is make your real numbers visible, and that is often the thing that surprises people most.

This guide is for social drinkers who want to drink a bit less, feel better the next day, and keep alcohol as something they choose rather than something that just happens. It is not a guide to recovery apps. If you think you need to stop drinking completely, or you get physical symptoms when you don't drink, skip to the section on when to talk to a doctor.

> **This is not medical advice.** Apps are tools for tracking and building habits. They are not treatment. **Talk to a doctor if** you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you go without a drink, you need a drink in the morning to feel normal, you have repeatedly tried to cut back and couldn't, or your drinking is causing problems with your health, work, or relationships. Stopping suddenly after a long stretch of heavy daily drinking can be dangerous, so get medical advice before you do it. In an emergency, call 911.

## What a "Mindful Drinking" App Actually Does

"Mindful drinking" is a loose term. It usually means paying attention to why, when, and how much you drink, and making each drink a choice instead of a habit. It sits somewhere between "drink whatever, whenever" and "never drink again." Plenty of people who use the term still drink regularly. They just drink on purpose.

Apps built around this idea tend to do some mix of five things:

1. **Tracking.** You log each drink, and the app turns that into weekly totals, standard drinks or units, calories, and money spent.
2. **Goal setting.** You pick a target, such as a number of drinks per week or a number of alcohol-free days, and the app shows how you're doing against it.
3. **Nudges and reminders.** A check-in text before the weekend, a reminder to log last night's drinks, a streak counter for dry days.
4. **Education.** Short lessons on how alcohol affects sleep, mood, and the body, or on handling social pressure to drink.
5. **Coaching or community.** Some paid apps offer access to human coaches, group sessions, or forums.

The first two are the core. Research on brief alcohol interventions (the short, structured conversations doctors use to help people cut back) has long found that seeing your own numbers next to a clear guideline helps many people drink less. Tracking apps are a self-serve version of that idea. Everything else is extra, and whether the extras are worth paying for depends on how you like to work.

## Cut-Back Apps vs. Recovery Apps

This matters because the two kinds of app are built for different people, and using the wrong one can feel off.

- **Cut-back (moderation) apps** assume you want to keep drinking but less, or with more alcohol-free days. They talk about weekly targets, planning nights out, and swapping some drinks for alcohol-free ones. Sunnyside, Drink Less, Drinkaware, and DrinkControl sit here. Reframe and Try Dry let you choose between cutting back and taking a break.
- **Recovery and sobriety apps** assume your goal is zero. They focus on sober streaks, milestone chips, and peer support for staying stopped. They can be great for people who have decided to quit, but if your goal is "two drinks on Saturday instead of six," the constant framing around sobriety can feel like it's for someone else.

If you're curious about taking a longer break, our guide to [being sober curious](/never-hungover/sober-curious) covers what that looks like without labels. If you just want to drink a bit smarter, our tips on [how to not get drunk](/never-hungover/how-to-not-get-drunk) pair well with any of the apps below.

## The Main Mindful Drinking Apps Compared

Prices and features change often, so check the app store listing before you subscribe. The table below covers what each app is built for and how it's generally priced.

| App | Best for | Cost model | Main features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Try Dry | Taking breaks and tracking year-round | Free | Drink diary, units, money and calories saved, dry-day goals |
| Drinkaware | Simple tracking against UK guidelines | Free | Drink logging, units, calories, weekly feedback |
| Drink Less | Evidence-focused cutting back | Free | Goals, tracking, self-monitoring tools developed by researchers |
| DrinkControl | Detailed personal tracking | Free with paid upgrades | Logs pure alcohol, calories, spending, charts and history |
| Sunnyside | People who want gentle nudges and a plan | Subscription, usually with a free trial | Weekly drink plan, text check-ins, tracking, coaching options |
| Reframe | People who like daily lessons and structure | Subscription, usually with a free trial | Daily program, tracker, community, coaching add-ons |

### Try Dry (Alcohol Change UK)

Try Dry is the official app of Dry January, made by the UK charity Alcohol Change UK. Despite the name, it isn't only for January. You can use it any time to log drinks, set dry days, and see how many units, calories, and how much money you've saved.

**Pros**

- Free, with no subscription upsell.
- Backed by a charity rather than a company trying to grow subscriptions.
- Clear, friendly design that makes dry days feel like a win rather than a test.
- Works well for structured breaks like Dry January or a "dry month."

**Cons**

- Built around UK units (one unit is 8 grams of alcohol), which can be confusing if you think in US standard drinks (14 grams).
- Less hand-holding than the paid apps. There's no daily coaching or text nudges.
- Its personality is strongly tied to the Dry January campaign, which some users who only want to moderate find less relevant.

### Drinkaware

Drinkaware is another UK charity, and its free app is a straightforward drink tracker. You log what you drink and it shows your units against the UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk guideline, which advises not regularly drinking more than 14 units a week and spreading those over three or more days.

**Pros**

- Free and simple.
- Compares your drinking to a clear official guideline, which is the most useful single piece of feedback a tracker can give.
- Shows calories, which is often the eye-opener for people focused on weight or fitness.

**Cons**

- Very UK-focused in units and guidance.
- Basic compared with the paid apps. If you want lessons, coaching, or a social feature, you won't find much here.

### Drink Less (University College London)

Drink Less was developed by behavioral scientists at University College London, and it has been studied in published trials, which is unusual for a consumer app. It includes goal setting, a drink diary, feedback on how your drinking compares with others, and tools aimed at building new habits.

**Pros**

- Free, with a research team behind its design.
- Built specifically for cutting back, not quitting.
- Focuses on the techniques with the best evidence, such as goal setting and self-monitoring.

**Cons**

- Designed with UK drinkers in mind, so units and comparisons are UK-based.
- The interface is functional rather than slick.
- Fewer extras than the commercial apps.

### DrinkControl

DrinkControl is a detailed tracker that logs drinks by volume and strength and calculates pure alcohol, calories, and money spent. It suits people who like data and want to see long-term trends.

**Pros**

- Works with any measurement system, so it's handy outside the UK.
- Good charts and history for spotting patterns, such as which nights of the week run heavy.
- The basic version is free.

**Cons**

- It's a tracker, not a coach. If logging alone doesn't change anything for you, it won't push further.
- Some features sit behind a paid upgrade.
- The detail can feel like homework if you just want a quick tap.

### Sunnyside

Sunnyside is a US-based app built around mindful drinking rather than sobriety. You set a weekly plan (for example, eight drinks and three dry days), and it checks in with you by text message to log drinks and stay on track. It also offers coaching options.

**Pros**

- Clearly built for moderation, with no assumption that you want to quit.
- Text check-ins lower the effort of logging, which is where most trackers fail.
- Weekly planning encourages you to decide in advance, which is easier than deciding mid-evening.
- Uses US standard drinks.

**Cons**

- It's a paid subscription after the trial, and the price is a real consideration for an app whose core job is tracking.
- Text messages can start to feel like noise, and some people tune them out after a few weeks.
- If you like detailed charts, a dedicated tracker may give you more.

### Reframe

Reframe offers a structured daily program of short lessons on how alcohol affects the brain and body, plus a drink tracker, exercises, a community forum, and coaching add-ons. You can set it up for cutting back or for quitting.

**Pros**

- Lots of content, which suits people who like to understand why habits form.
- Works for both moderation and longer breaks, so it can grow with your goals.
- Community features help if you like hearing from others making the same change.

**Cons**

- Subscription pricing, and the full value depends on actually doing the daily lessons.
- The volume of content can feel like a lot if all you wanted was a tracker.
- Because it serves people who are quitting too, some of the community and content leans toward sobriety.

## Do Mindful Drinking Apps Actually Work?

The honest answer is: modestly, for people who use them.

Reviews of digital alcohol interventions (apps and websites that give personalized feedback) have generally found small average reductions in how much people drink compared with getting no help or only general information. A 2017 Cochrane review of personalized digital interventions came to that kind of conclusion, while noting that the quality of evidence varied. The effect is real but not dramatic, and averages hide a lot: some people change a lot, many change a little, and plenty stop opening the app after a couple of weeks.

Research on Dry January, led by researchers at the University of Sussex, has suggested that many people who take part are still drinking less months later. Those studies rely on people who chose to sign up and report back, so they can't prove the challenge caused the change. Still, it fits a common pattern: a structured break with a clear start and end helps people notice how they feel without alcohol.

There is no good evidence that any one app is clearly better than the rest. The features with the strongest support across behavior-change research are:

- **Self-monitoring**, meaning tracking what you actually drink.
- **Specific goals**, such as "no more than eight drinks a week" rather than "drink less."
- **Feedback against a guideline**, so you know whether your normal is high.
- **Planning ahead**, deciding before the night out how many drinks you'll have.

Any app that makes those four things easy is doing the important work. Everything else is about whether you keep using it.

## How to Pick the Right App for You

Start by asking what usually derails you.

- **"I genuinely don't know how much I drink."** Start with a free tracker like Drinkaware, Try Dry, or DrinkControl. Log honestly for two weeks without trying to change anything. The numbers often do the persuading.
- **"I know the number. I just don't stick to my plan."** Look at an app with nudges and planning, such as Sunnyside, or set your own reminders before the nights that tend to run long.
- **"I want to understand why I reach for a drink."** Reframe's lesson-based approach, or the habit tools in Drink Less, suit this best.
- **"I want to take a month off."** Try Dry was built for exactly this.
- **"I don't want to pay."** Try Dry, Drinkaware, and Drink Less are all free, and a free tracker plus a clear weekly goal covers most of what the paid apps do.

A practical rule: try a free app first. If you find yourself logging consistently but still drifting past your goals, that's when a paid app with coaching or check-ins might earn its price. Most subscription apps offer a free trial, so use it fully before committing to an annual plan.

### Privacy is worth a minute

Drinking data is health data. Before you sign up, skim the privacy policy to see whether the app shares data with advertisers or third parties, whether you can delete your account and history, and whether it needs your contacts or location. Charity and university apps tend to collect less, but check each one rather than assuming.

## Getting Your Numbers Right: Standard Drinks and Units

Every tracker is only as good as what you put in, and the most common mistake is undercounting. A large pour of wine or a strong craft beer can be two standard drinks, not one.

- **In the US**, a standard drink contains 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly 12 ounces of 5% beer, 5 ounces of 12% wine, or 1.5 ounces of 40% spirits.
- **In the UK**, a unit is 8 grams of alcohol. A pint of 5% beer is nearly three units, and a large 250 ml glass of 13% wine is over three.

If your app lets you enter volume and strength, use that instead of picking "one beer." Our guide to [what counts as a standard drink](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) has a full breakdown by drink type, which makes logging much more accurate.

## Habits That Make Any App Work Better

The app is a mirror. These habits are what actually change the reflection.

1. **Log in the moment, or first thing the next morning.** Memory gets worse after a few drinks, and people consistently underestimate what they drank the night before.
2. **Set a weekly number, not a daily one.** It gives you room to have a bigger Saturday while still staying on target, and it makes dry days count.
3. **Plan your alcohol-free days in advance.** "Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday are dry" is easier to keep than deciding each evening.
4. **Decide your number before you go out.** Then tell a friend, or set the app's reminder. The decision made sober is the one to trust.
5. **Alternate with water or an alcohol-free drink.** It slows you down, helps with hydration, and gives you something in your hand.
6. **Watch the triggers.** Most trackers show patterns over time. If your heavy nights line up with stressful workdays or a particular group of friends, that's useful to know.
7. **Count wins, not just slips.** Seeing three dry days or a lower weekly total is motivating. A bad weekend is data, not failure.

For more on drinking in a way that fits your health goals, our [mindful drinking guide](/never-hungover/mindful-drinking-wellness-warrior-dhm-2025) goes deeper on the mindset side, and our [smart social drinking guide](/never-hungover/smart-social-drinking-your-health-first-strategies-guide-2025) covers practical strategies for nights out.

## What You'll Likely Notice When You Cut Back

People who use these apps often say the change they notice first isn't on the scale. It's the mornings. Fewer drinks usually means:

- **Better sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep but tends to break up sleep in the second half of the night, so cutting back often leads to more restful nights.
- **Fewer and milder hangovers.** The most reliable way to avoid a hangover is to drink less. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
- **Money saved.** Most trackers show this, and it adds up faster than people expect, especially with bar and restaurant prices.
- **Fewer empty calories.** A few drinks a night can add a surprising amount of energy intake over a week.

## When to Talk to a Doctor Instead of (or as Well as) an App

Apps are built for people who can change their drinking with a bit of structure. That covers most social drinkers. But some signs mean an app isn't the right tool on its own, and it's worth saying them plainly:

- **You feel physically unwell when you don't drink:** shaky hands, sweating, a racing heart, nausea, anxiety, or trouble sleeping that eases when you have a drink. These can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which needs medical advice. A bit of morning-after shakiness after one big night is different, and our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains that.
- **You need a drink in the morning** to feel steady or get going.
- **You keep setting goals and can't keep them,** even when you really want to.
- **Drinking is causing problems** with your health, work, money, or relationships.
- **You drink heavily every day** and want to stop. Stopping suddenly after a long period of heavy daily drinking can cause serious withdrawal, including seizures, so don't do it alone. A doctor can help you do it safely.

A doctor visit doesn't have to mean a big label or a program. Many primary care doctors are used to talking about drinking, and there are medications that can help some people cut back. In the US, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) runs a free website called Rethinking Drinking with tools to check your drinking pattern and a navigator to find professional help. In an emergency, such as confusion, a seizure, or someone who can't be woken, call 911.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

No supplement replaces drinking less. That's the only approach with solid evidence for fewer hangovers and better long-term health, and it's what these apps are for.

That said, some people who drink occasionally like to support their body on the nights they do. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it lets you drink more without consequences, and it shouldn't be used as a reason to drink past your goals. If you'd like to try it on the nights you drink, a well-reviewed budget option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- A mindful drinking app is mainly a tracker plus a goal. The free ones (Try Dry, Drinkaware, Drink Less, and DrinkControl's basic version) handle that well.
- Paid apps like Sunnyside and Reframe add nudges, lessons, and coaching. They're worth trying if you track consistently but still drift past your plan.
- Research suggests digital tools help people drink modestly less on average, mostly through tracking, clear goals, and planning ahead.
- Log honestly using real drink sizes, set a weekly target with planned dry days, and decide your number before you go out.
- If you get physical symptoms when you don't drink, need a drink in the morning, or can't stick to limits despite trying, talk to a doctor. An app isn't enough on its own in those cases.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best app for mindful drinking?**

There isn't one clear winner. For most people who want to cut back, a free tracker with a weekly goal is enough, and Try Dry, Drinkaware, and Drink Less are good free choices. Sunnyside suits people who want text check-ins and a weekly plan, and Reframe suits people who like daily lessons. Pick the one you'll actually open every week.

**Are there free apps to help you drink less?**

Yes. Try Dry (from Alcohol Change UK), Drinkaware, and Drink Less (developed at University College London) are free, and DrinkControl has a free basic version. They let you log drinks, set goals, and see your units or standard drinks, calories, and money spent. That covers the features with the best evidence behind them.

**Do drinking tracker apps really work?**

They tend to help modestly for people who keep using them. Reviews of digital alcohol tools have generally found small average reductions in drinking compared with no help. The parts that seem to matter most are tracking what you actually drink, setting a specific goal, comparing yourself with a clear guideline, and planning ahead. An app makes those easier, but it doesn't do them for you.

**Is Sunnyside or Reframe better for cutting back?**

They suit different styles. Sunnyside is built purely around moderation, with a weekly drink plan and text-message check-ins. Reframe offers a daily lesson program and community and works for either cutting back or quitting. Both are subscriptions with free trials, so try each before committing. If you mostly want tracking, a free app may be all you need.

**What's the difference between a mindful drinking app and a sobriety app?**

A mindful drinking app assumes you want to keep drinking but less, so it focuses on weekly targets, dry days, and planning. A sobriety app assumes your goal is to stop entirely and focuses on sober streaks and peer support for staying stopped. If your goal is moderation, a sobriety-focused app can feel like it's built for someone else.

**Can I use Try Dry outside of Dry January?**

Yes. Try Dry is the official Dry January app, but you can use it year-round to log drinks, set dry days, and track units, calories, and money saved. Many people use it for occasional breaks or to keep an eye on their weekly drinking.

**When should I see a doctor instead of using an app?**

Talk to a doctor if you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you go without a drink, need a drink in the morning, can't keep to the limits you set despite trying, or your drinking is causing problems. If you drink heavily every day, don't stop suddenly on your own, because withdrawal can be dangerous. A doctor can help you cut back safely.
